title: Akrura sees him in the river
hookLine: Akrura dives into the Yamuna and finds Krishna there too
carry: the lord is in the chariot and the river

lines: THE CHARIOT STOPS AT THE RIVER.
THE BOYS ARE IN THE WATER.
cards: On the road to Mathura, the chariot stops at the river. Akrura asks the boys to wait in the shade while he goes down to the Yamuna to bathe and say his prayers. He wades in, ducks under, and opens his eyes.
Krishna and Balarama are there, under the river, looking at him. Which is strange, because he just left them sitting in the chariot.

teach.h: ON THE CHARIOT, AND IN THE RIVER.
teach.b: He comes up for air and looks back at the bank. There's the chariot, and the two boys sitting in it, just as he left them. So he goes under again, and this time the vision is bigger.

He sees Balarama as the great serpent Ananta, and resting on him, Vishnu himself, dark as a rain cloud, with sages singing his praise. Akrura stays there in the river, and the Bhagavata gives him a long hymn of praise.
Then he climbs out, dripping, and walks back to the chariot in a daze.

Krishna asks him, kindly, whether he's seen something wonderful, Akrura answers that every wonder there is, is in Krishna, and he's looking at him. Why put this scene here? The village has just watched Krishna leave.

And on that same road, a man finds that the boy in the chariot is also in the river, and also beyond all of it. This is one of Hinduism's biggest teachings, told as a story: the Lord isn't in one place.

teach.h: VISHNU: THE ONE WHO PERVADES EVERYTHING.
teach.b: Vishnu's very name is often explained as the one who pervades everything. Hindus keep a murti at home and go to the temple to meet him there, but they don't believe that's the only place he is.
The leaving is real; nobody in the story pretends it isn't.

But many readers hear the river as the answer to the grief: the one who left the village hasn't left anything. They reach Mathura as the day ends, and Krishna walks into the city on foot, with the cowherds.

how: Akrura's hymn in the Bhagavata is recited by devotees, and pilgrims bathe at a place on the Yamuna that tradition links with his vision.

the road to Mathura, and Akrura's vision in the river

games.q: you're Akrura. under the river you see the two boys you just left in the chariot. you come up and they're still in the chariot. what do you do?
o: decide it was the light on the water.
go back under and look again.
hurry back to the chariot and say nothing.
games.why: Akrura goes under again, and this time sees Vishnu resting on Ananta. the boy in the chariot is in the river too: the Lord isn't in one place.

practice: Akrura met the Lord while bathing and praying, and many Hindus still begin the day with water and a name. As you wash today, go slowly.

If you pray, say softly, Om Namo Narayanaya, or Krishna's name, or the name of God you use, remembering he's in that water too. If you don't pray, just look at the water as if you'd come up from the river.

wordCard.voice: Leaving Vrindavan. The journey to Mathura, where Akrura sees the boys on the chariot, and also in the river, and Vishnu beyond them.

orig.note: Sanskrit and Hindi: Mathura, Kamsa's city on the Yamuna, where the chariot is headed.

carryVoice: Your line: the Lord is in the chariot and the river. Akrura looked twice and saw him everywhere. That's day nine hundred four.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 10.39–10.41, Akrura's vision in the Yamuna, his hymn, and the arrival at Mathura
